fields.independence_analysis: The three competing assertions draw on three distinct original records. The 1850 census (a_002, src_001) and the 1860 census (a_009, src_003) are independent as sources — different years, different enumerators, different documents. However, for the specific birthplace fact, both census records most likely trace to the same pool of informants: Thomas Flynn or his wife, the only household members present across both enumerations who would have reported Patrick's birthplace. The underlying knowledge behind both census entries may therefore be the same family tradition, even though the source records are formally independent. This means the two census assertions together deserve somewhat more weight than a single census, but they cannot be treated as fully independent corroboration — they are better understood as two separate recordings of a single informant group's claim. The 1908 death certificate (a_012, src_004) is fully independent of both censuses: a different record type, a different institution, a different informant (James Brown, son-in-law), and a different era. The three assertions thus represent two substantive information streams: (1) the Flynn household's reported birthplace across two censuses, and (2) James Brown's recollection on the death certificate.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors decisively favor the census assertions reporting Ireland. First, informant proximity: whoever reported Patrick's birthplace in the 1850 and 1860 censuses — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — had firsthand knowledge of where their child was born. James Brown, by contrast, was a son-in-law who could not have witnessed Patrick's birth and was reporting a fact about events that occurred roughly 60 years before the 1908 death certificate was filed. A son-in-law is not a primary informant for birth facts. Second, contemporaneity: the 1850 census was recorded when Patrick was approximately five years old, and the family was actively living as a unit. The 1860 census confirmed the same birthplace ten years later. The death certificate was created 58 years after the first census, by an informant at one remove from the family of origin. Third, consistency across independent occasions: two separate enumerations, in different decades and recorded by different government employees, both returned Ireland as the birthplace. That two recordings from the household agree is meaningful even accounting for their partial informant dependency. The defensible rationale for setting aside a_012 is a combination of (2) more error-prone source — secondary informant with no firsthand knowledge — and (3) substantially less credible evidence for this particular fact given the informant's epistemic distance from Patrick's birth.
fields.resolution_rationale:
Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute between Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) and Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate). Resolving this matters because the birthplace — Ireland vs. Pennsylvania-born of Irish parents — affects where to search for corroborating immigration records and bears on the family's origin narrative.

Two original census records state Ireland as Patrick's birthplace: the 1850 Schuylkill County census (Patrick listed as age 5, birthplace Ireland) and the 1860 Schuylkill County census (Patrick listed as age 15, birthplace Ireland). Both are original government records, recorded by census enumerators who visited the Flynn household. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate — also an original government record — states Pennsylvania as the birthplace, with James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, identified as the informant.

The census entries are more reliable for the birthplace fact. The household informant in 1850 and 1860 — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — had direct, firsthand knowledge of where Patrick was born. They were present at or near the birth and were reporting from lived experience while the family was intact. James Brown, the 1908 informant, was a son-in-law who could not have witnessed Patrick's birth some 63 years earlier. He was reporting from secondhand knowledge — what he had been told, or what he believed — about a fact he had no independent way to verify. Two consistent household recordings from different decades outweigh one later recollection by a family member at one remove.

The most plausible explanation for the Pennsylvania entry is immigration-origin confusion by a secondary informant: James Brown knew Patrick had spent his entire adult life in Pennsylvania and may have conflated Patrick's long Pennsylvania residence with his birthplace. This is a well-documented pattern — when a son-in-law who knew his father-in-law only as a Pennsylvanian was asked where Patrick was born, the locally familiar answer was Pennsylvania, and the correct answer (Ireland, from a time before Brown knew the family) was not part of his knowledge. The preferred assertion is a_002 (1850 census, birthplace Ireland), supported by a_009 (1860 census, same claim).

Patrick Flynn's birthplace is in dispute between Ireland (1850 and 1860 censuses) and Pennsylvania (1908 death certificate). Resolving this matters because the birthplace — Ireland vs. Pennsylvania-born of Irish parents — affects where to search for corroborating immigration records and bears on the family's origin narrative.

Two original census records state Ireland as Patrick's birthplace: the 1850 Schuylkill County census (Patrick listed as age 5, birthplace Ireland) and the 1860 Schuylkill County census (Patrick listed as age 15, birthplace Ireland). Both are original government records, recorded by census enumerators who visited the Flynn household. The 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate — also an original government record — states Pennsylvania as the birthplace, with James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, identified as the informant.

The census entries are more reliable for the birthplace fact. The household informant in 1850 and 1860 — almost certainly Thomas Flynn or his wife — had direct, firsthand knowledge of where Patrick was born. They were present at or near the birth and were reporting from lived experience while the family was intact. James Brown, the 1908 informant, was a son-in-law who could not have witnessed Patrick's birth some 63 years earlier. He was reporting from secondhand knowledge — what he had been told, or what he believed — about a fact he had no independent way to verify. Two consistent household recordings from different decades outweigh one later recollection by a family member at one remove.

The most plausible explanation for the Pennsylvania entry is immigration-origin confusion by a secondary informant: James Brown knew Patrick had spent his entire adult life in Pennsylvania and may have conflated Patrick's long Pennsylvania residence with his birthplace. This is a well-documented pattern — when a son-in-law who knew his father-in-law only as a Pennsylvanian was asked where Patrick was born, the locally familiar answer was Pennsylvania, and the correct answer (Ireland, from a time before Brown knew the family) was not part of his knowledge.

Two U.S. Census records — one from 1850 and one from 1860 — both record Patrick Flynn's birthplace as **Ireland**. The 1908 death certificate says **Pennsylvania**. Here's why the discrepancy exists and how it was resolved:

---

**Why the death certificate says Pennsylvania**

review_dimensions.name: Source independence analysis
review_dimensions.rationale: Claude's independence analysis is specific and grounded in the informant chain. It correctly identifies that the 1850 and 1860 censuses are independent as records (different enumerators, ten years apart) but partially dependent as evidence (same household informant—likely Thomas Flynn—for age and name facts on both occasions). It correctly identifies the 1908 death certificate as fully independent (different institution, different informant James Brown, no derivation from either census). Critically, it addresses the 'household 197, age 6' candidate by name, noting it has no corresponding assertion, log entry, or search result, and therefore does not constitute an independent evidence unit. This is exactly the specificity the dimension requires.

review_dimensions.name: Evidence weighing
review_dimensions.rationale: Claude applies the GPS preponderance hierarchy with specific grounding. It cites the 1850 and 1860 records as original sources (outweighing derivative), notes the death certificate as original and direct (a_013 directly states 'Father: Thomas Flynn'), and emphasizes temporal continuity (age 5 in 1850 → age 15 in 1860 → death ~age 63 in 1908, all consistent with one person). No facts are asserted beyond what the record carries.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants would outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. That weighing has not been done: c_001 is unresolved, no preferred assertion is recorded, and this conclusion adopts no birthplace.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

fields.independence_analysis: The identity question turns on three bodies of evidence: (1) the 1850 census placing Patrick Flynn, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (src_001, original); (2) the 1860 census placing Patrick Flynn, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household, same county, ten years later (src_003, original); and (3) the 1908 death certificate naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father (src_004, original). The 1850 and 1860 censuses are independent original records created by different enumerators ten years apart. The death certificate is a third independently created original, with a different informant (son-in-law James Brown). All three rest on different underlying acts of recording and different informants. The 1850 Ancestry derivative (src_002) is not independent of src_001 — it is a transcription of the same original — so it adds no separate weight. The three originals are genuinely independent of one another for the purpose of identity.
fields.weighing_analysis: Two factors are decisive. First, the 1860 census is the most important piece: it places Patrick Flynn, age 15, in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household ten years after the 1850 enumeration, with an age (15) perfectly consistent with the 1850 age (5). A continuous ten-year co-enumeration with the same household head, consistent ages, and the same county constitutes strong affirmative evidence that the Patrick in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household and the Patrick in his 1860 household are the same person — and therefore the same person who died in Schuylkill County in 1908. Second, the 1908 death certificate directly names Thomas Flynn as the deceased's father. The informant (son-in-law James Brown) is secondary for birth and parentage facts, but naming the father is a concrete fact about family identity that a son-in-law living in the same community could readily know from decades of family life, even without firsthand birth knowledge. This direct statement corroborates the census co-enumeration pattern. The second Patrick Flynn (household 197, age 6) has no subsequent records tying him to the 1908 death certificate subject, no corroborating census placements with Thomas Flynn, and no document naming Thomas Flynn as his father.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The question is whether the Patrick Flynn enumerated in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household (dwelling 84, age 5) is the same person whose 1908 death certificate is in evidence. A second Patrick Flynn of similar age appeared in Schuylkill County's 1850 census (household 197, age 6), creating the ambiguity.

The 1850 census, the 1860 census, and the 1908 death certificate together provide three independent lines of evidence. The 1850 census places Patrick Flynn, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household. The 1860 census independently places Patrick Flynn, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household in the same county — an age perfectly consistent with the 1850 enumeration and representing ten years of continuous co-residency with the same household head. The 1908 death certificate, created by a different authority entirely (the Pennsylvania Department of Health), directly names Thomas Flynn as the deceased Patrick Flynn's father.

The 1860 census is the most powerful evidence: it positively places our Patrick Flynn with Thomas Flynn across a ten-year span, ruling out the possibility that the Thomas Flynn household's 1850 Patrick was a transient who bore no ongoing relationship to that family. The death certificate's explicit naming of Thomas Flynn as father locks the link between the 1908 decedent and the Thomas Flynn household.

The second Patrick Flynn (household 197, 1850) lacks any corroborating record tying him to Thomas Flynn as father or to the 1908 death certificate subject. His subsequent trajectory is entirely undocumented in this research. Absence of evidence is not itself proof he is a different person, but the positive chain — 1850 Thomas Flynn household → 1860 Thomas Flynn household → 1908 death naming Thomas Flynn as father — is an affirmative identification that does not depend on the competing candidate's disappearance. The identification is confirmed by the convergence of three independent original sources.

fields.independence_analysis: The identity question turns on three bodies of evidence: (1) the 1850 census placing Patrick Flynn, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (src_001, original); (2) the 1860 census placing Patrick Flynn, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household, same county, ten years later (src_003, original); and (3) the 1908 death certificate naming Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father (src_004, original). The 1850 and 1860 censuses are independent original records created by different enumerators ten years apart. The death certificate is a third independently created original, with a different informant (son-in-law James Brown). All three rest on different underlying acts of recording and different informants. The 1850 Ancestry derivative (src_002) is not independent of src_001 — it is a transcription of the same original — so it adds no separate weight. The three originals are genuinely independent of one another for the purpose of identity.
fields.weighing_analysis: Two factors are decisive. First, the 1860 census is the most important piece: it places Patrick Flynn, age 15, in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household ten years after the 1850 enumeration, with an age (15) perfectly consistent with the 1850 age (5). A continuous ten-year co-enumeration with the same household head, consistent ages, and the same county constitutes strong affirmative evidence that the Patrick in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household and the Patrick in his 1860 household are the same person — and therefore the same person who died in Schuylkill County in 1908. Second, the 1908 death certificate directly names Thomas Flynn as the deceased's father. The informant (son-in-law James Brown) is secondary for birth and parentage facts, but naming the father is a concrete fact about family identity that a son-in-law living in the same community could readily know from decades of family life, even without firsthand birth knowledge. This direct statement corroborates the census co-enumeration pattern. The second Patrick Flynn (household 197, age 6) has no subsequent records tying him to the 1908 death certificate subject, no corroborating census placements with Thomas Flynn, and no document naming Thomas Flynn as his father.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The question is whether the Patrick Flynn enumerated in Thomas Flynn's 1850 household (dwelling 84, age 5) is the same person whose 1908 death certificate is in evidence. A second Patrick Flynn of similar age appeared in Schuylkill County's 1850 census (household 197, age 6), creating the ambiguity.

The 1850 census, the 1860 census, and the 1908 death certificate together provide three independent lines of evidence. The 1850 census places Patrick Flynn, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household. The 1860 census independently places Patrick Flynn, age 15, in the same Thomas Flynn household in the same county — an age perfectly consistent with the 1850 enumeration and representing ten years of continuous co-residency with the same household head. The 1908 death certificate, created by a different authority entirely (the Pennsylvania Department of Health), directly names Thomas Flynn as the deceased Patrick Flynn's father.

The 1860 census is the most powerful evidence: it positively places our Patrick Flynn with Thomas Flynn across a ten-year span, ruling out the possibility that the Thomas Flynn household's 1850 Patrick was a transient who bore no ongoing relationship to that family. The death certificate's explicit naming of Thomas Flynn as father locks the link between the 1908 decedent and the Thomas Flynn household.

The second Patrick Flynn (household 197, 1850) lacks any corroborating record tying him to Thomas Flynn as father or to the 1908 death certificate subject. His subsequent trajectory is entirely undocumented in this research. Absence of evidence is not itself proof he is a different person, but the positive chain — 1850 Thomas Flynn household to 1860 Thomas Flynn household to 1908 death naming Thomas Flynn as father — is an affirmative identification that does not depend on the competing candidate's disappearance. The identification is confirmed by the convergence of three independent original sources, none of which traces to the other Patrick Flynn.

output.text_response:
Here is the conflict-resolution agent's full response:

---

**A note on terminology:** "Primary" and "secondary" describe the *informant's proximity to the event* — not the source itself. "Original" and "derivative" describe the *physical document* — whether it is the record as first created or a later copy/index/transcription.

---

**Source 1: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County (src_001)**
Classification: **Original document.** The FamilySearch digital image reproduces the NARA microfilm of the original population schedule as written by the enumerator in 1850.

| Assertion | Fact | Informant classification | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_001 | Patrick's name | **Indeterminate** | The enumerator recorded the name, but who stated it — a household member or a neighbor — cannot be established from the record. The informant is unknown. |
| a_002 | Birth (~1845, Ireland) | **Indeterminate** | Age and birthplace had to be told to the enumerator by someone. That person was most likely a household member, but the census does not identify who. If it was Thomas Flynn or his wife, it would be secondary information (they were present at the birth but Patrick himself had no cognitive memory of it). Because the informant is unidentifiable, it is classified indeterminate. |
| a_003 | Residence in Schuylkill County, 1850 | **Primary** | Residence is uniquely the one census fact for which the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling. No informant statement needed. |
| a_004 | Relationship (child inferred in Thomas Flynn household) | **Indeterminate / researcher inference** | The 1850 census has no relationship column. This assertion is a researcher inference from household position and shared surname, not a statement any informant made. There is no informant to classify. |

---

**Source 2: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County (src_003)**
Classification: **Original document.** Same situation as above — FamilySearch image of the original NARA microfilm population schedule.

| Assertion | Fact | Informant classification | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_010 | Relationship (child inferred in Thomas Flynn household, 1860) | **Indeterminate / researcher inference** | The 1860 census also lacks an explicit relationship column (that was not added until 1880). Again, a researcher inference — no classifiable informant. |

---

**Source 3: 1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate (src_004)**
Classification: **Original document.** The certificate is the official record as created at the time of death; the FamilySearch image is of the original held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

A death certificate typically has **multiple informants contributing different facts**, and the classification follows each fact's informant, not the document as a whole:

| Assertion | Fact | Informant classification | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_013 | Father: Thomas Flynn | **Secondary** | The informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law. He would not have had firsthand knowledge of his father-in-law's parentage — he was reporting what he had been told. His epistemic distance from the event (Patrick's birth) is at least one generation removed, and Patrick had already died, so no correction was possible. |

The source notes also flag this correctly: the certificate is primary for death facts (date, place, cause — all recorded close to the event by the attending physician and registrar), but secondary for birth and parentage facts supplied by the son-in-law informant.

---

**Summary**

- All three sources are **original documents** — none are indexes, transcripts, or derivative compilations.
- **Primary information** appears in only one assertion: the residence fact (a_003), where the enumerator's own visit is the evidence.
- **Secondary information** appears in a_013: the father's name as told by the son-in-law on the death certificate.
- **Indeterminate information** is the dominant classification across the census assertions (a_001, a_002, a_010) because the actual informant who spoke to the enumerator cannot be identified from the records.
- **Researcher inferences** (a_004, a_010) fall outside the primary/secondary framework entirely — no informant made those statements; the researcher constructed them from household structure.

The weakest evidence for the parentage question (q_001) is therefore **a_013**, the only directly stated parentage claim — it rests on a secondary informant (the son-in-law) with no firsthand knowledge of the fact it asserts. If you want to move toward a proof conclusion on Patrick's parentage, the death certificate's naming of Thomas Flynn is a piece of evidence, but it cannot stand alone given its informant's epistemic position.

entry.description: ParentChild conflict surfaced by tree_edit when adding I3 (Thomas Flynn, Luzerne County) as Patrick Flynn's (I1) father via the 1845 baptism (a_018). Two competing Thomas Flynn candidates are asserted as Patrick's father: I2 (Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County, a_004) and I3 (Thomas Flynn, Luzerne County, a_018). The question is whether the Thomas Flynn named as Patrick's father on the 1845 Luzerne County baptism record is I2, I3, or a third individual.
entry.identity_question: Is the Thomas Flynn named as Patrick Flynn's father on the 1845 Wilkes-Barre baptism record the same person as I2 (Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, found in 1842 Philadelphia marriage and 1850/1860 Schuylkill censuses) or I3 (Thomas Flynn of Luzerne County, found in the 1840 Luzerne census and dead by 15 September 1840)?

fields.independence_analysis: Three source streams bear on this identity question. First, the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County census records (a_004, a_010) both place a Thomas Flynn as head of the household containing Patrick Flynn, and both derive from different enumerators in different years — they are independent original sources on co-residence, though the inferred parent-child relationship in each rests on the same structural logic (shared surname, household position) rather than a stated fact. Second, the 1845 Wilkes-Barre baptismal register (a_018) is an independent original source that explicitly names Thomas Flynn as father. Third, I3's death record (a_016) and the 1840 Luzerne census (a_014) are independent original sources documenting I3's life and death in Luzerne County. The Philadelphia 1842 marriage record (a_017, linked to I2) is independent of all of the above. No source for the I3 candidate derives from the I2 stream or vice versa — the independence is not in question. The analytical problem is chronological, not evidentiary: one candidate is documented as dead before the baptism occurred.
fields.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor is biological plausibility, the seventh weighing factor (plausibility given historical fact). I3 (Thomas Flynn, Luzerne County) died 15 September 1840 per a primary-quality county death record (a_016) — a record created near the time of death by an official witness. The baptism of Patrick Flynn is dated 3 August 1845, nearly five years after I3's recorded death. A deceased man cannot father a child born five years after his death. No calendar conversion can close this gap: both records are American civil records kept in Gregorian reckoning, and the largest possible Julian-to-Gregorian offset for the 19th century is 13 days — a rounding error against a 1,782-day interval. I3 is therefore eliminated on a fundamental biological assumption (persons cannot act after death), not merely outweighed. By contrast, I2 (Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County) is documented alive in 1842 (Philadelphia marriage, a_017) and in 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill censuses — a continuous living presence that spans the 1845 baptism date. The baptism is recorded in Luzerne County (Wilkes-Barre), adjacent to Schuylkill County, a geographically plausible location for a family that later appears in Schuylkill County. The person-evidence link of a_018 to I3 (pe_010) was made on place alone and is speculative by its own rationale, while the link to I2 through the census stream (pe_002, pe_006) rests on continuous documented co-residence.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The dispute concerns whether the Thomas Flynn named as Patrick Flynn's father on the 1845 Wilkes-Barre baptism is I2 (Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill County) or I3 (Thomas Flynn, Luzerne County). The resolution is required to add the correct paternal edge to the tree without a competing-parent collision.

The competing evidence: a_004 infers a parent-child relationship between Patrick (I1) and Thomas (I2) from household position in the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill County censuses — an indirect, inferred assertion based on shared surname and co-residence. Assertion a_018 is a direct, stated assertion from the 1845 St. Nicholas Church baptismal register in Wilkes-Barre, which names Thomas Flynn as father from information provided by the parents or sponsors present at the baptism — a primary-quality original source for parentage.

I3 is eliminated by chronological impossibility. The Luzerne County death record (a_016) is a primary-quality original source documenting Thomas Flynn of Luzerne County died 15 September 1840. The baptism was recorded 3 August 1845 — four years and ten months later. Because no man can father a child after his own death, I3 is disqualified as the father named on the baptism, regardless of the geographic coincidence that both I3 and the baptism are associated with Luzerne County. This is not a weighing judgment; it is a biological impossibility that removes I3 from consideration entirely.

The baptism (a_018) therefore names I2 as Patrick's father. I2 is documented alive in 1842 (Philadelphia marriage) and continuously through the 1850 and 1860 Schuylkill censuses, spanning the 1845 baptism date. The Wilkes-Barre location is geographically adjacent to Schuylkill County and consistent with a family that settled there by 1850. The baptism's explicit, primary-quality naming of Thomas Flynn as father outweighs the indirect census-cohabitation inference of a_004 in any case — a stated entry in a church register at the moment of baptism, by an officiating priest recording from the parents present, is the stronger evidence for parentage.

The speculative pe_010 link of a_018 to I3 was made on place alone and must be corrected: a_018 belongs to I2, not I3. The preferred assertion for the winning parentage claim is a_018 (the baptism's direct statement), supported by the census co-residence evidence of a_004. The tree edge should connect I2 as Patrick's father, and person-evidence should be updated to reassign a_018 from I3 to I2.

The probability that an enumerator in an 1875 Norwegian census substituted one patronymic for another by clerical error — writing Pedersen for Hansen — is low; these are phonetically and visually distinct, and patronymics were the primary identifying element of a person's name. The shared given name (Anders) and matching age (~7) and district (Ringsaker) are suggestive but not sufficient to override this signal: the name Anders was common in Norway, the traditional first-son naming pattern (named for the paternal grandfather) means multiple families in the same district could produce an Anders around 1868, and census age figures carry a margin of a year or two.
added.resolution_rationale:
The fact at issue is whether a single census entry — 1875 Ringsaker, 'Anders Pedersen', age 7 — belongs to the research subject Anders Hansen (b. ~1868, son of Hans Olsen). Linking this record to the subject would materially change what we know about his early life; an incorrect link would import a stranger's parentage and origins into the subject's record.

The census entry records the name 'Anders Pedersen' (a_001) and age 7 in Ringsaker, Hedmark (a_002). The research subject's established patronymic is Hansen, derived from his father Hans Olsen. The census persona's patronymic Pedersen derives from a father named Peder — a different man.

In 1875 Norway, patronymics were the operative, government-recorded surname system; the fixed-surname law did not arrive until 1923. An enumerator writing 'Pedersen' was making a precise, meaningful statement: this child's father is named Peder. Writing Hansen for the same child would be a categorical error, not a phonetic slip, because the two names are structurally and aurally distinct. The shared given name and matching age are consistent with a same-district coincidence: Anders was a common Norwegian given name, traditional naming patterns (first son named for the paternal grandfather) could produce multiple Anders-aged-7 boys in one district, and census ages carry an inherent margin of one to two years.

The most defensible conclusion is that these are two distinct individuals: one Anders Pedersen (son of a Peder) and the research subject Anders Hansen (son of Hans Olsen), both approximately seven years old in 1875 Ringsaker. The patronymic mismatch, under the naming system confirmed by the FamilySearch Norway Naming Customs page as fully operative at this date, disqualifies the census entry as a record of the subject. However, because the conflict rests on a single source with no independent corroboration on either side, the exclusion is a strong inference rather than a proved conclusion.

What would make this definitive: (1) a Ringsaker church baptismal register entry from approximately 1867–1869 naming Anders Hansen, son of Hans Olsen — this would positively identify the subject in the same parish and make the census match unnecessary; (2) similarly, a baptismal entry for an Anders Pedersen, son of a Peder, in Ringsaker ~1867–1869 would confirm the census child as a distinct person; (3) any household schedule listing Hans Olsen with children, which could show whether Anders Hansen appears elsewhere in the 1875 census under his correct patronymic. Until one of these records surfaces, 'these are different persons' is the reasoned finding but cannot be declared fully proved.

fields.independence_analysis: The evidence bearing on the identity question comes from four distinct sources: the 1850 census (src_001, original), the 1860 census (src_003, original), the 1908 death certificate (src_004, original), and the research log recording the scope of the 1850 census search (log_001). The 1850 and 1860 censuses are independent originals — different enumerations ten years apart, different enumerators, different pages — and they are independent of the death certificate, which was created 58 years after the 1850 census by a different party (son-in-law James Brown) reporting what he knew of Patrick's parentage. The 1850 census record and the Ancestry derivative (src_002) are NOT independent: Ancestry's transcription traces directly to the same original enumeration, so they count as one evidential unit. The candidate second Patrick Flynn mentioned in c_002's description (household 197, age 6) has no corresponding assertion in this project; the search log states 'Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match,' meaning the enumerator found no surviving indexed record of a same-named rival candidate who passed an age/location filter. The search evidence is therefore one unit (the negative result of the 1850 search) that cannot be independently verified from project data, though it is consistent with the FamilySearch, Ancestry, and MyHeritage searches all returning the same household without surfacing a second candidate.
fields.weighing_analysis: Three factors are decisive. First, the death certificate directly names Thomas Flynn as father (a_013). This is the most relevant record type for parentage — it expressly states the relationship rather than implying it from household position. Though the informant (son-in-law James Brown) is secondary for birth facts, parentage of the deceased was something he could reasonably have known from family knowledge and from Patrick himself during Patrick's lifetime; the 1908 date means Patrick lived until adulthood, and his own son-in-law had decades to learn who his father-in-law's father was. Second, the 1860 census provides an independent ten-year follow-up showing Patrick Flynn age 15 still living in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (a_008/a_010). Continuity of co-residence across two census years is strong corroboration that the 1850 co-enumeration reflects a genuine parent-child relationship, not a coincidence of names. Third, the search log (log_001) explicitly examined eight 1850 results and found no other Patrick Flynn of matching age in Schuylkill County — the household 197 candidate described in c_002 did not survive the age/location filter across FamilySearch, Ancestry, and MyHeritage searches. No assertion for a second candidate appears in the project. In the absence of a documented rival candidate with evidence of the same quality, the three convergent sources (1850, 1860, death certificate) support the same conclusion: the Patrick in Thomas Flynn's household is our subject.
fields.resolution_rationale:
The question is whether the Patrick Flynn listed as a child in Thomas Flynn's 1850 Schuylkill County household (dwelling 84, age 5) is the same person as the Patrick Flynn whose 1908 death certificate is the anchor record for this research. The conflict description notes a possible second Patrick Flynn in household 197 (age 6), which, if it were a real rival candidate, would make the assignment to dwelling 84 uncertain.

The competing evidence consists of: (1) the 1850 census entry in Thomas Flynn's household (a_001), which places a Patrick Flynn age 5 in Schuylkill County; (2) the 1860 census, which places a Patrick Flynn age 15 — consistent with the 1845 birth year — still living in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household (a_008/a_010); (3) the 1908 death certificate (a_013), which names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father and gives Schuylkill County as the place of death, fully consistent with life-long residence there; and against these, the c_002 description's reference to a second Patrick Flynn in dwelling 197 (age 6) — an individual for whom no assertion exists in this project and who did not survive the multi-repository search filter.

The identity link to Thomas Flynn's 1850 household is supported by all three independent original sources. The 1860 census is ten years after 1850 and independently confirms the same parent-child household, making coincidence of two unrelated Patrick Flynns in the same family implausible. The death certificate is the most direct evidence: it names Thomas Flynn as the father, corroborating that the Thomas-Patrick household link is genuine, not an artifact of same-name ambiguity. The informant (son-in-law James Brown) had decades of contact with Patrick and could plausibly have known his father-in-law's parentage.
